prompt.context: Our client, FlyMe.com, is a US-based online travel agency (OTA) — similar to Expedia, Priceline, etc. They sell flights, hotel rooms, car rentals, and other travel products on their website directly to consumers. Their inventory comes from all of the major travel suppliers (airlines, hoteliers, car rental companies, etc.). Although the travel industry is large and growing, our client has recently experienced a drop in profitability. They have hired us to (1) figure out why profits are down, and (2) what they can do to turn around the business.
prompt.question: Why are profits down at FlyMe.com, and what should the client do to turn around the business?

clarifying_info.a: Primary sources of revenue are booking fees charged to suppliers for each sale, and banner advertising revenue on the website.
Mostly in the US; they have some subsidiaries elsewhere but they are small.
A broad range of products — flights, hotels, car rentals, cruises, trip insurance — from a broad range of providers.
Very well-known; a household name in the US.
5–6 main competitors in the US. 2 are profitable; the rest are experiencing declines similar to FlyMe.com. The industry has seen recent consolidation.

clarifying_info.q: What is happening on the cost side?
clarifying_info.a: Overall costs have been growing ~3% year over year. Growth is happening across most key categories.

clarifying_info.q: Have end ticket prices to consumers changed?
clarifying_info.a: No, end ticket prices to consumers have stayed the same.

exhibits.title: FlyMe.com Selected Financial Data — 2013 & 2014
exhibits.shows: A table comparing 2013 and 2014 revenue (in $M) and bookings (in millions) across six product/revenue lines: Air, Hotel, Car Rental, Cruise, Banner Ad Revenue, and Trip Insurance Revenue.

framework: Revenue: Break down by product (Air, Hotel, Car Rental, Cruise, Banner Ads, Trip Insurance); analyze Price (booking fee per sale) × Quantity (bookings volume) for each
Costs: Fixed vs. variable; assess whether cost growth is abnormal or inflationary
Root cause identification: Determine which revenue or cost driver is responsible for the profit decline
Turnaround levers: Identify actionable ways to recover lost revenue or improve margins
Supplier/competitive dynamics: Assess buyer-supplier power, competitive pricing pressure, and consolidation trends

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 1. What do the numbers tell you about the revenue trend?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute total revenue for each year: 2013 = $440+$270+$75+$15+$150+$50 = $1,000M; 2014 = $319+$331+$81+$17+$149+$53 = $950M — a ~$50M decline. Candidate should then identify Air as the single largest product by 2013 revenue and note its dramatic drop. Strong candidates flag that overall Air bookings volume actually increased (110M→159M) while Air revenue fell sharply, implying the booking fee per transaction fell significantly.

math.setup: Calculate average booking fee per product per year = Revenue / Bookings
math.answer: The ~$50M revenue shortfall is driven almost entirely by the collapse in the Air booking fee (from ~$4.00 to ~$2.01 per booking), even as Air booking volumes grew 45%. All other product lines are flat or growing.

questions.prompt: What could be causing the drop in air booking fees?
questions.guidance: Hypothesis-driven brainstorm. Strong candidates justify each idea and quickly converge on competitive/supplier-power explanations. Interviewer reveals: 'A lot of factors contributed, but we had to drop the air booking fees to stay competitive — there was nothing we could do.'

brainstorming.prompt: Given that air booking fees dropped due to competitive pressure and nothing could be done to prevent it, what can FlyMe.com do to improve revenues?

categories.name: Causes of air booking fee drop (first brainstorm)
ideas: Airlines have strong bargaining power and pressured OTAs to drop fees
Contract renewals occurred and the new rate is lower
Airlines are selling more flights directly on their own websites; FlyMe had to drop fees to keep inventory
Air ticket prices are dropping overall, compressing percentage-based fees
Mix shift toward low-cost carriers (Spirit, Frontier) with lower-priced tickets
A competitor dropped booking fees and FlyMe had to follow suit

categories.name: Product / mix shift
ideas: Focus growth efforts on Hotel bookings — booking fee is high ($9–$11) and rising
Push Trip Insurance sales aggressively — revenue per booking is ~$25–$27, the highest of all products
Bundle air bookings with hotel and car rental to drive volume to higher-margin products

categories.name: Revenue growth
ideas: Increase advertising spend to drive more traffic, boosting overall bookings and banner ad revenue
Invest in CRM and personalization to improve conversion rates and repeat bookings
Expand into new travel verticals (tours, experiences, vacation packages) with better margins

categories.name: Competitive / structural
ideas: Consolidate with a competitor to increase bargaining power against airlines
Develop a loyalty program to reduce customer acquisition costs and increase lifetime value
Build direct supplier relationships or exclusive inventory deals to differentiate from competitors

recommendation: Profits are down ~$50M due to a collapse in the Air booking fee (from ~$4.00 to ~$2.01 per booking), driven by competitive pressure from airlines and OTA rivals — not a cost problem

FlyMe.com should pursue a bundling strategy — anchoring air bookings with hotel and car rental add-ons — to shift revenue mix toward higher-margin products (Hotel ~$10/booking, Trip Insurance ~$26/booking)
Simultaneously, invest in growing hotel and trip insurance penetration rates as the highest-margin product lines
risks: Bundling may reduce overall air booking conversion if customers resist add-ons
Hotel and trip insurance markets may also face competitive fee pressure over time
Competitors could undercut on hotel/insurance fees as they did on air
Execution risk: sales and marketing capabilities may need significant investment
next_steps: Quantify the revenue uplift from a bundling strategy using current attach-rate data
Assess whether hotel and trip insurance supplier contracts allow margin expansion
Evaluate M&A targets among the 3–4 unprofitable US OTA competitors to gain scale and bargaining power
Model the impact of increased marketing spend on traffic and bookings across high-margin products
